name: Coverage Gaps
purpose: Topics no existing learner covers well: data science/ML, UI/UX design, DevOps/infra, personal productivity. Should trigger brain-level coverage gap and 'create' evolution decisions.
items: Studying transformer architectures. Attention mechanism makes intuitive sense — weighting input focus — but multi-head and positional encoding are still fuzzy.
Trained simple LSTM on support ticket data to predict priority. 73% accuracy. False positive rate for 'critical' too high — predicting everything as critical.
Embeddings: words, sentences, images as dense vectors in high-dimensional space where distance correlates with semantic similarity. Elegant concept.
Fine-tuning a small language model on our API docs with LoRA. Goal: internal chatbot that answers 'how do I use endpoint X?' questions.
Bias-variance tradeoff in practice. Our recommendation model has high variance — performance varies wildly between users. Need more data or regularization.
UX research methods: usability testing (can they use it?) vs user interviews (should we build it?). We do neither. Starting with 5 interviews per sprint.
Nielsen heuristics for interface design are timeless. 'Visibility of system status' — our app has no loading states, progress indicators, or success confirmations.
Gestalt principles: proximity, similarity, continuity, closure. Explains why settings page feels chaotic — related options aren't grouped. Proximity fixes 80%.
Color accessibility: 8% of men have color vision deficiency. Our errors rely solely on red text. Adding icons and labels alongside color.
Progressive disclosure: show only what's needed at each step. Registration form has 12 fields on one page. Breaking to 3 steps of 4 reduced competitor's abandonment by 40%.
Setting up Kubernetes. Learning curve is steep but abstractions make sense: pods, services, deployments, ingress. YAML is verbose — considering Helm.
Prometheus + Grafana monitoring. Tracking RED method (request rate, error rate, duration) plus business metrics: signups/hour, checkout completion.
Infrastructure as code with Terraform. Every cloud resource version-controlled and reproducible. No more 'someone clicked in the AWS console.'
Chaos engineering: intentionally injecting failures to build resilience. Starting small: randomly killing one pod per day in staging to verify health checks.
GitOps with ArgoCD. Push to main → auto-deploy staging. Push tag → deploy production. Entire deployment state in git. Rollback = revert commit.
Pomodoro technique for deep work. 25 minutes focused, 5 minute break. Consistently more done in 4 sessions (2 hours) than 8 hours of context switching.
Deep Work by Cal Newport. Focused uninterrupted work is rare and valuable. Blocking 9am-12pm as no-meetings time. Those 3 hours exceed the rest.
Energy level journaling. Peak creativity: 9-11am. Execution: 2-4pm. Low: after lunch, after 5pm. Aligning task types to windows makes big difference.
'Eat the frog' — hardest task first. Works 60% of the time. Other 40%, the frog is too ambiguous and I need a warmup task for momentum.
Time-boxing meetings to 25 minutes instead of 30. 5-minute buffer is transformative. People get breaks and don't start meetings frazzled.
Learning about random forests for our fraud detection system. The ensemble approach — many weak classifiers voting — is surprisingly robust against overfitting.
Confusion matrix analysis on our spam filter. Precision is 95% but recall is only 60%. We're missing 40% of spam. Adjusting the classification threshold.
Feature engineering insight: raw timestamps are useless to ML models. Extracting hour-of-day, day-of-week, and is-holiday as separate features dramatically improved accuracy.
K-means clustering on user behavior data revealed 4 distinct user segments we didn't know existed. One segment uses the product in a way we never designed for.
Cross-validation: splitting data into 5 folds and training/testing on each. Our initial 95% accuracy dropped to 78% with proper validation. We were overfitting.
Reading about attention mechanisms in NLP. The key insight: not all input tokens are equally important for a given output. Self-attention learns which tokens to focus on.
Experimenting with vector databases (Pinecone) for semantic search. Instead of keyword matching, we're matching by meaning. Relevant results even when the exact words don't match.
The information architecture of our app is a mess. Users can't find settings, help, or their saved items. Card sorting exercise with 10 users revealed our mental model doesn't match theirs.
Learned about Fitts's Law: the time to reach a target is proportional to the distance and inversely proportional to the size. Our most-used button is tiny and in the corner. Moving it.
Responsive design audit. Our app breaks on screens narrower than 380px. 12% of mobile users have smaller screens. Fixing the viewport assumptions in our grid system.
Color theory in UI: using complementary colors for CTAs, analogous colors for content sections. Our monochrome scheme makes every element equally prominent — nothing stands out.
Micro-interactions matter more than I thought. Adding a subtle animation when an item is saved (0.3s scale bounce) reduced 'did it save?' support tickets by 30%.
Typography hierarchy: we use 3 font sizes and 1 weight. Adding a proper type scale (6 sizes, 2 weights) made the information hierarchy immediately scannable.
Form UX: inline validation as users type is annoying. Validate on blur (when they leave the field). Show success states too, not just errors. Users need positive feedback.
Mobile touch targets: minimum 44x44 pixels per Apple HIG. Our mobile nav links are 28px tall. No wonder users tap the wrong item. Increasing to 48px.
Dark mode implementation: it's not just inverting colors. Need to adjust contrast ratios, shadow behavior, image brightness, and status colors independently.
Kubernetes pod autoscaling based on custom metrics. Instead of CPU, scaling on request queue depth. More responsive to actual load patterns. Handles traffic spikes 40% faster.
Terraform state management in teams. Remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking. Prevents two engineers from modifying infrastructure simultaneously.
Multi-region deployment architecture. Primary in us-east-1, failover in eu-west-1. Database replication lag is 200ms. Acceptable for reads, not for writes.
Service mesh with Istio. Automatic mTLS between services, traffic management, observability. The operational complexity is significant but security posture improved dramatically.
Container image scanning in CI with Trivy. Found 23 high-severity CVEs in our base images. Switched from node:18 to node:18-slim, reduced to 3 CVEs.
Learned about the OODA loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) for incident response. Our team skips 'Orient' — we jump from observing a problem to acting without understanding context.
Implemented SLOs (Service Level Objectives) with error budgets. 99.9% availability = 43 minutes of allowed downtime per month. When budget is spent, we freeze feature work and fix reliability.
Personal knowledge management with Zettelkasten method. Each note is atomic, interconnected with others. After 3 months, emergent connections between ideas I never would have seen.

The Eisenhower matrix for task prioritization: urgent+important (do), important+not-urgent (schedule), urgent+not-important (delegate), neither (eliminate). 60% of my tasks were in the 'delegate' quadrant.
Spaced repetition for retaining technical knowledge. Using Anki for cloud architecture patterns. 10 minutes daily, and I actually remember the AWS service limits during incident response.

Second brain methodology (building a personal knowledge base): capture everything interesting, organize by actionability, distill the key insights, express by creating new work. The 'distill' step is where the learning happens.

Morning routine experimentation: wake at 6, no phone for first hour, 20 minutes reading, 10 minutes journaling. Felt gimmicky at first but the clarity at 7am is noticeably different than starting with email.
Working memory is limited to ~4 chunks. When debugging complex systems, I now externalize state: write down what I know, what I'm testing, and what I expect. Prevents 'what was I doing?' moments.
The two-minute rule: if a task takes less than 2 minutes, do it now. Applied to code reviews — if a PR is <20 lines, review immediately instead of adding to the review queue.
Batch processing personal tasks like email. Checking email 3x daily instead of continuously. Each session is more focused and I respond more thoughtfully.
AWS Lambda cold starts are killing our user experience. First request after idle: 3.2 seconds. Implemented provisioned concurrency for critical paths. Cost $40/month but latency is now consistent.
Database connection pooling with PgBouncer. Our 4 app servers each had 20 connections = 80 total. PostgreSQL max_connections was 100. PgBouncer pools them, effectively infinite app-side connections.
Nginx tuning: increased worker_connections from 1024 to 4096, enabled keepalive to upstream, tuned proxy buffers. Throughput up 35% with no code changes.
Migrated from self-hosted RabbitMQ to AWS SQS. Lost some features (message priority, complex routing) but gained: zero ops burden, auto-scaling, 5 nines availability.
Log retention policy: 7 days hot (Elasticsearch), 90 days warm (S3 + Athena), 1 year cold (S3 Glacier). Reduced logging costs from $2000/month to $300/month.
Network policy in Kubernetes: by default, every pod can talk to every other pod. Implemented deny-all default with explicit allow rules. Reduced blast radius of any single compromised pod.
CDN configuration for our single-page app. index.html: no-cache (always fresh). Static assets (JS, CSS, images): immutable, 1 year cache with content hash in filename.
Learned about distributed consensus (Raft protocol). Understanding how leader election and log replication work made me appreciate why distributed databases have the limitations they do.
SSL/TLS certificate rotation automation with cert-manager in Kubernetes. No more 'certificate expired' incidents at 3am. Certificates auto-renew 30 days before expiry.
Read about cognitive load theory applied to code. High intrinsic load (problem complexity) + high extraneous load (bad code structure) = overwhelmed developer. We can only reduce extraneous load.
The paradox of choice in developer tools. Evaluated 6 different state management libraries for 3 weeks. Should have picked one in day 1 and committed. Analysis paralysis is real.
Walking meetings for 1-on-1s. Something about moving physically while talking makes difficult conversations easier. Plus we both get away from screens for 30 minutes.
Learned about the Dreyfus model of skill acquisition: novice → advanced beginner → competent → proficient → expert. Most developers are 'competent' but think they're 'expert'. Self-awareness matters.
Focus music experiment: tried lo-fi, classical, ambient, and silence. Silence wins for complex problems. Lo-fi wins for repetitive tasks. Classical is too distracting.
Implementing feature stores for ML. Centralized repository of pre-computed features that training and serving pipelines share. Eliminates training-serving skew.
A/B test pitfall: we declared a winner after 3 days with p=0.04. But we checked the results 7 times during those 3 days. Multiple testing correction required — actual significance was p=0.15.
Data pipeline orchestration with Airflow. DAGs define dependencies between tasks. Retry logic, alerting, and backfill capabilities built in. Our cron-based pipeline was a house of cards.
Anomaly detection using isolation forests. No need for labeled data — it finds outliers by measuring how easy they are to isolate via random partitioning. Caught 3 fraudulent accounts this week.
The data quality problem: garbage in, garbage out. Our ML model accuracy fluctuates because upstream data sources randomly change formats. Added data contracts and schema validation at ingestion.

Implementing RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) for our support chatbot. Embed documentation → store in vector DB → retrieve relevant chunks → feed to LLM with context. Much better than fine-tuning.
User session recording analysis (Hotjar). Discovered users try to click our chart legends expecting them to filter. They're decorative, not interactive. Quick fix: make them interactive.
Design sprint: 5 days from problem to tested prototype. Day 1: map the problem. Day 2: sketch solutions. Day 3: decide. Day 4: prototype. Day 5: test with 5 users. Compressed months into a week.

Accessibility audit with screen reader (VoiceOver). Our app is nearly unusable — missing alt text, unlabeled buttons, broken tab order, no skip-to-content links. 20% of fixes took an hour; 80% took a week.

The 'jobs to be done' framework: users don't buy products, they hire them for a job. Our users don't want 'project management software' — they want 'to never miss a deadline.' Reframing changes everything.

Motion design principles: ease-in for entering elements, ease-out for exiting, spring physics for interactive elements. Our current animations are all linear — feels robotic. Small curves make it feel alive.
Kubernetes horizontal pod autoscaler was slow to react (5 minute lag). Switched to KEDA with Prometheus metrics. Scaling happens within 30 seconds of load change.
Infrastructure cost optimization: found 3 oversized EC2 instances, 2 unused Elastic IPs, and a forgotten test cluster. Monthly savings: $1,200. Set up cost alerts for any resource over $50/month.
Learning about WebAssembly for compute-intensive frontend tasks. Ported our client-side image processing from JavaScript to Rust+Wasm. Processing time: 2.3 seconds → 180ms.
Observability vs monitoring: monitoring tells you when something is wrong; observability tells you why. Invested in distributed tracing and structured events rather than more dashboards.
Zero-trust networking: never trust, always verify. Even internal services authenticate to each other. Eliminated our flat network where any compromised service could access everything.
